claim: A visit-count bonus of order N^-1/2 (pseudo-count from a density model) turns a deep RL agent into an explorer on sparse-reward Atari: Montezuma's Revenge, 15 of 24 rooms by 50M frames, one run 6600 points by 100M frames (5 trials, beta 0.05). Original claim, but it was tuned on this game.
agent_test: Keep a code-side table of directions tried (key = normalised direction label) and add a 1/sqrt(n+0.01) preference when choosing the next S3 direction; compare coverage of distinct correct answers at equal tokens against plain resampling.

claim: The count idea survives swapping the density model and using other keys: PixelCNN pseudo-counts beat CTS pseudo-counts in 52/57 games by max score and 51/57 by AUC; SimHash counts with TRPO double Freeway (16.5 to 31.6) and lift Frostbite (2869 to 4683); RND reaches Montezuma 8152 vs PPO 2497. Several independent groups agree that some novelty-by-count signal helps sparse games.
agent_test: Compare three keys for the history table (exact string, normalised operator plus approach label, embedding hash) on the same item set at equal tokens.

claim: What the key is decides success: raw pixel hashing at fine granularity treats every state as new (Frostbite), learned or task-relevant keys (autoencoder code, BASS) do better on Montezuma/Venture, and ICM/RND avoid counting uncontrollable noise.
agent_test: Run the history table with keys at coarse vs fine granularity; measure duplicate-direction rate and answer coverage.

claim: The gain is not only the bonus: the mixed Monte Carlo return matters as much as the bonus in the hardest games (neither alone gives significant benefit, together they do), and gains were larger once bonus scale was raised 1-2 orders of magnitude (best runs 6600 Montezuma, 39000 Private Eye).
agent_test: Ablate the history table against a table plus a separate credit-assignment trick; keep each only if it wins at equal tokens (G7).

claim: Bonus-based exploration does not generalise as headline results suggested: in a fair Rainbow re-test (200M frames, 5 seeds, tuned on Montezuma) bonuses help on Montezuma (CTS reaches 5000, others 2500, epsilon-greedy poor) but Montezuma rank does not correlate with other hard games, epsilon-greedy beats the bonuses on Gravitar, and on the easy training set pseudo-count is worse on every game except Seaquest.
agent_test: Tune any novelty bonus on one problem class only, then test on three other classes at equal tokens; keep it only if it does not lose on easy classes (supports G12 spend-by-difficulty).

claim: Prediction-error bonuses stall on unpredictable states (noisy TV): a noisy-TV in a Unity maze drastically slows ICM-style learning, and a dynamics-error agent is significantly worse than RND on Montezuma, Private Eye and Solaris; once extrinsic reward is exhausted RND agents keep chasing bonus ('dancing with skulls').
agent_test: Gate any novelty term in S3 by code: stop adding novelty bonus once a verified pass exists, and exclude surface variation (wording changes) from the novelty key.

claim: Counts alone are not enough at the top end: Go-Explore (archive of cells, return then explore) gets mean 43,763 on Montezuma without domain knowledge and 666,474 with it, versus 8,152 for RND; NGU (episodic kNN novelty times lifelong RND) and Agent57 combine episodic and lifelong novelty and an adaptive bandit over exploration weight.
agent_test: At S6 impasse, return to the best partial attempt in an archive (keyed by the history table) and extend it, versus restart from scratch, at equal tokens.

claim: Count-style intrinsic reward has a real but small effect on LLM reasoning RL: MERCI (learned pseudo-counts on reasoning trajectories) lifts Qwen2.5-Math-7B GRPO mean@k average 40.5 to 42.2 and DAPO 42.2 to 44.9, pass@k average 65.8 to 67.4. The gain is concentrated in AIME (AIME25 pass@256 50.0 to 60.0, 30 problems so 3 problems); Minerva and MATH500 pass@16 do not improve (64.0 to 63.2, 91.8 to 91.4). Without noise filtering it falls below baseline (63.8 vs 65.8). One paper. Gap search: no per-benchmark replication found; Qwen-math RLVR gains are confounded by spurious-reward effects (random reward +21.4 vs +29.1 on MATH-500).
agent_test: Replicate on our task set with a history-table bonus; report per-benchmark, not only the average.

claim: Hash-based pseudo-counts on chain-of-thought embeddings fail in LLMs: most responses fall into the same or neighbouring hash cells, so counts are uninformative; the CDE authors switched to a perplexity bonus (Qwen3-4B-Base GRPO average 48.2 to 50.6) and a critic-variance bonus. Gap search: keys that work in LLM work are a judge-labelled strategy cluster (Hu 2026) or a covariance bonus on hidden states (Tuyls 2025), not hashes.
agent_test: Measure collision rate of an embedding hash over our S3 attempts; if above half, use a symbolic key (operator, approach label) instead.

claim: Plain LLM agents explore poorly without scaffolding: GPT-4 with a basic prompt shows suffix failure (best arm never chosen after early rounds) in over 60% of bandit replicates (T=100); only GPT-4 with chain-of-thought and an externally summarised history avoided it. Summarising history in code is what helped. Gap search: EVOLvE (summary stats in prompt), Harris and Slivkins 2026 (LLMs help propose candidates, worse than regression at exploiting, raw history degrades) and Monea 2025 (positive-only subsampled episodes) agree that code-made summaries beat raw history.
agent_test: Compare passing raw attempt history vs a code-built count summary to the S3 generator, at equal tokens.

claim: Standard RLVR narrows rather than widens what an LLM can solve at large k: RL model about 30% above base at small k but base wins at large k (Minerva 32B about 9% at k=128); training pass@1 26.1 to 42.5 while pass@256 falls. Indirect evidence that LLM exploration is weak and that entropy loss is only part of the cause.
agent_test: Measure distinct-answer coverage at k=1,8,64 for plain sampling vs table-guided S3 at equal tokens.

claim: Raw novelty rewards (count, RND, APT) waste effort in large open environments because most novelty is irrelevant; LLM-judged goals or tasks (ELLM, OMNI, Voyager curriculum) give better-aligned coverage. Voyager: random curriculum cuts discovered items by 93% (not re-opened).
agent_test: Note G8: novelty is judged by running, not by model opinion. Test table-count novelty plus code-run validity against LLM-judged interestingness on open-ended items.

claim: Count-based UCB is regret-optimal in bandits and the tabular MBIE-EB bonus beta/sqrt(N) has PAC-MDP bounds; Bellemare's Theorem 1 ties the pseudo-count bonus to information gain (IG <= PG <= 1/N). These are tabular results; Kolter and Ng and Strehl and Littman were not opened, and they do not carry to LLM attempt spaces without a notion of state.
agent_test: None directly; use only as the rationale for a 1/sqrt(n) shape and compare with a flat penalty on repeats.

claim: Longer reasoning traces help exploration only when redundancy is penalised: LIE (length reward plus redundancy penalty) reports +4.4% in-domain and +2.7% out-of-domain; this conflicts with G11 (think briefly) unless the extra length is spent on non-repeated directions.
agent_test: At equal tokens compare one long attempt with a redundancy penalty vs several short independent attempts (G11).

claim: A count bonus on the final outcome helps at test time only in refined form: naive UCB on outcomes raised training reward but gave a significant test gain only for Llama-8B on the easy set (3 seeds); a within-batch repetition penalty improved pass@k at large k. Because checkable answers have deterministic reward, a refuted answer should be excluded, not just discounted.
agent_test: Compare a hard 'refuted outcome' list against a 1/sqrt(n) discount for the same items at equal tokens.

claim: The key granularity that works in LLM exploration papers is semantic: an LLM-judged strategy cluster (inverse cluster size reward, Qwen2.5-7B AIME AUC@64 0.131 to 0.160 vs SimpleRL 0.116) or a hidden-state covariance bonus (over 50% better samples-to-correct for Qwen-2.5-14B), while exact text is always new and embedding hashes collapse.
agent_test: Use an LLM call to label each attempt's approach, keep counts in code, and compare to exact-string and embedding-hash keys.

claim: Whether to push novelty or refine depends on difficulty: sequential revision beats parallel resampling on easy MATH items, parallel or tree search wins on hard ones, beam search hurts easy items at high budget, and a naive revision model flips about 38% of correct answers to wrong. Supports gating novelty by S0 difficulty and freezing verified answers.
agent_test: Run the table on and off per S0 difficulty class and measure the rate of correct-to-wrong flips.

claim: Return-to-archive with an LLM choosing the state and keeping a per-state list of tried actions beats ReAct, Reflexion and classic visit-count Go-Explore in text environments (Game of 24: 100% vs 38 +/- 22 for visit-frequency Go-Explore; removing the action history drops it to 33 +/- 9), at equal environment operations, not tokens.
agent_test: At S6 impasse compare extending the best partial attempt with restart, at equal tokens.

claim: Conditioning generation on earlier attempts with an instruction to be different raises diversity of correct solutions (DivSFT: AST edit distance 0.072 to 0.264, pass@100+ up 10.8 to 12.5 points on code), but this is evidence after fine-tuning and abstract-level only; the plain independent-resampling baseline already gives large coverage gains (Large Language Monkeys: CodeContests Gemma-2B 0.02% to 7.1%).
agent_test: Prompt-only: show a short code-made list of tried approaches and ask for a different one, versus independent samples at equal tokens.
